idiom_name: extension trait: local trait + blanket impl (IteratorExt style)
implementation_notes: Rust forbids inherent impls on foreign types (a type may only be given inherent methods in its own crate), so the servant is a local trait carrying the behaviour plus an impl for the serviced types, conventionally one blanket impl over the capability - the extension trait idiom used across the ecosystem (itertools::Itertools, futures::StreamExt). The capability interface is the supertrait or bound (Movable), and the extension methods appear with member syntax only in modules that import the trait. Choose it when call-site readability matters; the trait's methods are ordinary static function calls once compiled, so there is no runtime cost.
pitfalls: The methods exist only where the trait is in scope: a missing use gives 'no method named move_to found for ...' at the call site, and re-exporting through a prelude module is the usual fix.

A blanket impl covers every type meeting the bound and cannot be specialised afterwards (coherence), so state the bound exactly; a too-wide impl offers methods that fail only when called on the wrong type.
sources: The Rust Reference, Implementations - inherent implementations must be in the crate that defines the type, which is why extension traits exist; https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/implementations.html
Rust RFC 0445, Extension Trait Conventions - the pattern, the Ext naming convention and the blanket-impl form; https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/0445-extension-trait-conventions.html

Comprehensive Rust (Google), Extension Traits - worked example of adding methods to a foreign type through a local trait; https://google.github.io/comprehensive-rust/idiomatic/leveraging-the-type-system/extension-traits.html

variants.name: Trait-bounded free function (classic servant)
variants.idiom_name: generic free function `fn move_to<T: Movable>(t: &mut T, to: Position)`
variants.implementation_notes: The literal translation of the pattern: the servant is a generic free function whose bound names the capability, called as move_to(&mut shape, pos). Nothing new is added to the serviced type, so the behaviour cannot collide with a method, cannot be accidentally found as a member, and the call site shows exactly which servant acts - useful when several servants provide similarly named operations or when the trait must stay private. It composes as well as the extension trait (the bound is just a bound) and avoids importing a trait at every call site at the price of losing method syntax and fluent chains.
pitfalls: Without method syntax the servant is invisible from the type's documentation and callers must know it exists: name and re-export it deliberately (a module per service) rather than leaving it in a catch-all utils module.
Generic bounds are monomorphised per type, so a servant instantiated for many serviced types grows code size; take &dyn Movable when the call is not hot and the set of serviced types is open.
sources: The Rust Reference, Implementations - trait implementations as the way to attach behaviour; https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/implementations.html
Microsoft, Rust Training: Traits in Depth - blanket impls, bounds and the trade-off against extension traits; https://microsoft.github.io/RustTraining/rust-patterns-book/ch02-traits-in-depth.html
